## Appendix B Missing Details and Proofs

### B.1 More Definitions

#### Definition 2 (Second-order stationary point).

A point $X_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ is a second-order stationary point of $f_{w}$ if

$$ \begin{gathered}\nabla f_{w}(X_{w})=0,\\
\nabla^{2}f_{w}(X_{w})[D,D]\geq 0\quad\text{for every }D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}.\end{gathered} $$

We write $M_{w}=X_{w}X_{w}^{\top}$ .

#### Definition 3 (Restricted isometry).

The operator $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies $(\delta,s)$ -RIP if

$$ (1-\delta)\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{A}(Z)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{F}^{2} $$

for every $Z\in\mathbb{S}^{n}$ with $\rank(Z)\leq s$ .

#### Assumption 1 (Unified $2k$ -RIP).

Unless stated otherwise, $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies $(\delta,2k)$ -RIP for a fixed $\delta\in[0,1)$ . Since $r_{\star}\leq k$ , this assumption covers all rank-at-most- $2k$ symmetric matrices used below, including differences between rank-at-most- $k$ PSD matrices. We set $s_{\rm RIP}=2k$ throughout.

For $M\succeq 0$ , let its nonzero eigenvalues be

$$ \lambda_{1}(M)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{\rank(M)}(M)>0. $$

When an effective active rank $q$ is selected, $P_{q}(M)$ denotes the projector onto the top- $q$ eigenspace and $P_{q}^{\perp}=I-P_{q}$ . The tangent space of the rank- $q$ PSD manifold at a rank- $q$ matrix with range projector $P$ is

$$ \mathcal{T}(P)=\{\eta\in\mathbb{S}^{n}:\;P^{\perp}\eta P^{\perp}=0\}. $$

Every $\eta\in\mathcal{T}(P)$ has rank at most $2q$ .

### B.2 Missing Details of Section 4

#### Lemma 1 (Factor Hessian identity).

Let $M=XX^{\top}$ . For every $D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla^{2}f_{w}(X)[D,D] \displaystyle=\left\lVert\mathcal{A}(XD^{\top}+DX^{\top})\right\rVert_{2}^{2} \displaystyle+2\left\langle G_{w}(M),DD^{\top}\right\rangle. $$

Moreover, $X$ is first-order critical iff

$$ G_{w}(M)X=0. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 1.

The first and second variations of $XX^{\top}$ in direction $D$ are

$$ \eta=XD^{\top}+DX^{\top},\qquad 2DD^{\top}. $$

Applying the chain rule to $F_{w}(XX^{\top})$ gives the gradient $2G_{w}(M)X$ and the quadratic form (48). ∎

#### Remark 2 (Order of magnitude of chart constants).

The raw chart is well conditioned when the active spectrum is bounded: if $0<c\leq\lambda_{k}(M_{w})\leq\lambda_{1}(M_{w})\leq C$ , then $\kappa_{\rm raw}(M_{w})=O(1)$ . If $\lambda_{k}(M_{w})=\varepsilon\ll 1$ while $\lambda_{1}(M_{w})=O(1)$ , then $\kappa_{\rm raw}(M_{w})=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1})$ . If $\lambda_{1}(M_{w})=L\gg 1$ and $\lambda_{k}(M_{w})=\Omega(1)$ , then $\kappa_{\rm raw}(M_{w})=\Theta(L)$ . These scalings are coordinate geometry, not RIP. RIP controls $\mathcal{A}$ on tangent matrices, but it does not control the conditioning of a raw SVD/graph chart near the rank-deficient boundary.

#### Proposition 1.

Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}$ have rank $q$ , let $M=XX^{\top}$ , let $P$ be the range projector of $M$ , and assume $G_{w}(M)X=0$ . For any factor direction $D$ producing the tangent matrix

$$ \eta=XD^{\top}+DX^{\top}\in\mathcal{T}(P), $$

the factor Hessian obeys

$$ \nabla^{2}f_{w}(X)[D,D]\geq\left(\alpha_{T}(P)-\rho_{q}^{-}(M;w)\right)\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

Consequently, under Assumption 1,

$$ \nabla^{2}f_{w}(X)[D,D]\geq\left(1-\delta-\rho_{q}^{-}(M;w)\right)\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Write $M=U\Lambda U^{\top}$ , where $\Lambda=\diag(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{q})$ and $\lambda_{q}>0$ . Since $XX^{\top}=M$ and $X$ has full column rank, after a right-orthogonal change of factor coordinates we may take $X=U\Lambda^{1/2}$ . Decompose a factor perturbation as

$$ D=UA+U_{\perp}B. $$

Then

$$ \eta=U(\Lambda^{1/2}A^{\top}+A\Lambda^{1/2})U^{\top}+U\Lambda^{1/2}B^{\top}U_{\perp}^{\top}+U_{\perp}B\Lambda^{1/2}U^{\top}. $$

The normal block of $DD^{\top}$ is

$$ P^{\perp}DD^{\top}P^{\perp}=U_{\perp}BB^{\top}U_{\perp}^{\top}. $$

Since $G_{w}(M)X=0$ , the range and cross terms of $G_{w}(M)$ vanish, so

$$ \left\langle G_{w}(M),DD^{\top}\right\rangle=\left\langle P^{\perp}G_{w}(M)P^{\perp},U_{\perp}BB^{\top}U_{\perp}^{\top}\right\rangle. $$

Let $K=B\Lambda^{1/2}$ . The off-diagonal block of $\eta$ is $K$ , hence

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\geq 2\left\lVert K\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, \displaystyle\tr(BB^{\top}) \displaystyle=\tr(K\Lambda^{-1}K^{\top}) \displaystyle\leq\frac{\left\lVert K\right\rVert_{F}^{2}}{\lambda_{q}}\leq\frac{\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2}}{2\lambda_{q}}. $$

Therefore

$$ 2\left\langle G_{w}(M),DD^{\top}\right\rangle\geq-\frac{\left\lVert[P^{\perp}G_{w}(M)P^{\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{q}}\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

The first term in (48) is at least $\alpha_{T}(P)\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2}$ , proving (50). The RIP specialization follows from (7). ∎

#### Assumption 2 (RIP-certified endpoint Hessian lower margin).

Let $M_{w}\in\mathcal{M}_{k}$ satisfy (10), and set

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{w} \displaystyle=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w), \displaystyle\lambda_{w} \displaystyle=\lambda_{k}(M_{w}),\qquad P_{w}=P_{k}(M_{w}), \displaystyle\gamma_{w} \displaystyle=\left\lVert P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Equivalently,

$$ \rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w)=\frac{\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp})\}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{w})}. $$

We assume $\mu_{w}>0$ .

#### Assumption 3 (Small noise relative to the endpoint scale).

With $\mu_{w},\lambda_{w},\gamma_{w}$ from Assumption 2, define the computable endpoint variation scale

$$ \mathfrak{L}_{w}=\frac{2(1+\delta+\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w))}{\lambda_{w}}+\frac{16\gamma_{w}}{\lambda_{w}^{2}}, $$

with the convention that $\mu_{w}/(4\mathfrak{L}_{w})=+\infty$ if $\mathfrak{L}_{w}=0$ . The noise obeys

$$ \frac{2\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\mu_{w}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}r_{w}^{\rm stab},\qquad r_{w}^{\rm stab}=\min\left\{\frac{\lambda_{w}}{4},\frac{\mu_{w}}{4\mathfrak{L}_{w}}\right\}. $$

#### Why the margin cannot be dropped.

If the endpoint Hessian has a flat eigen-direction, linear robustness can fail even in one dimension. Consider

$$ \phi_{0}(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^{4},\qquad\phi_{\varepsilon}(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^{4}-\varepsilon x. $$

The unperturbed critical point is $x_{0}=0$ , but $\phi_{0}^{\prime\prime}(0)=0$ . The perturbed critical point solves

$$ \phi_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(x)=x^{3}-\varepsilon=0,\qquad x_{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon^{1/3}. $$

Thus $\left\lvert x_{\varepsilon}-x_{0}\right\rvert=\varepsilon^{1/3}$ , which is not bounded by $C\varepsilon$ for any fixed $C$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ . A positive margin is exactly what rules out this flat-bottom behavior and lets the criticality equation be inverted.

#### Lemma 2 (Small-noise critical-point continuation).

Suppose Assumptions 1–3 hold. Then there exists a $C^{1}$ curve

$$ s\mapsto M_{s}\in\mathcal{M}_{k},\qquad 0\leq s\leq 1, $$

with $M_{1}=M_{w}$ , such that every $M_{s}$ is a rank- $k$ critical point of $F_{s}$ :

$$ \grad_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})=0. $$

Moreover, along this branch,

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\eta,\Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})[\eta]\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq\frac{\mu_{w}}{2}\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}^{2},\qquad\eta\in T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}, \displaystyle\lambda_{k}(M_{s}) \displaystyle\geq\frac{\lambda_{w}}{2}. $$

We call $M_{0}:=M_{s=0}$ the paired clean endpoint.

#### Proof of Lemma 2.

Let $\pi(X)=XX^{\top}$ . At every full-column-rank factor $X$ , the differential

$$ \mathrm{D}\pi_{X}[D]=XD^{\top}+DX^{\top} $$

is surjective onto $T_{M}\mathcal{M}_{k}$ , where $M=\pi(X)$ . Its kernel is the vertical space generated by the right-orthogonal invariance:

$$ \ker(\mathrm{D}\pi_{X})=\{X\Omega:\Omega^{\top}=-\Omega\}. $$

Thus, after removing these representation-induced vertical directions, factor perturbations provide horizontal lifts of all tangent directions on $\mathcal{M}_{k}$ . The factor–manifold Hessian comparison of Luo et al. (2025, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1) then transfers the curvature lower bound in Proposition 1 to the Riemannian Hessian. Assumption 2 therefore implies that $\Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{w}(M_{w})$ is positive definite on $T_{M_{w}}\mathcal{M}_{k}$ . The implicit-function theorem on the embedded manifold now yields a local critical branch in the parameter $s$ (Absil et al. 2008, Proposition 5.5.6); (Boumal 2023, Proposition 5.45).

It remains to show that the branch cannot leave the endpoint neighborhood before reaching $s=0$ . Let $P=P_{k}(M)$ and suppose $\left\lVert M-M_{w}\right\rVert_{F}\leq r\leq\lambda_{w}/4$ . Weyl’s inequality gives $\lambda_{k}(M)\geq 3\lambda_{w}/4$ , and Davis–Kahan gives $\left\lVert P-P_{w}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2r/\lambda_{w}$ (Davis and Kahan 1970; Bhatia 1997). Since $G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}=0$ , the endpoint gradient is purely normal:

$$ G_{w}(M_{w})=P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}. $$

Using

$$ G_{s}(M)=G_{w}(M_{w})+H(M-M_{w})+(1-s)N_{w}, $$

RIP and Cauchy–Schwarz give, for every unit vector $v$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}H(M-M_{w})v\right\rvert \displaystyle=\left\lvert\left\langle\mathcal{A}(vv^{\top}),\mathcal{A}(M-M_{w})\right\rangle\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert M-M_{w}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

because $vv^{\top}$ has rank one and $M-M_{w}$ has rank at most $2k$ . Also $\left\lvert v^{\top}N_{w}v\right\rvert\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}$ . Let

$$ b_{w}=\left\lVert[P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\lambda_{w}\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w). $$

Projector rotation changes the endpoint normal block by at most

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert P^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P^{\perp}-P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 2\gamma_{w}\left\lVert P-P_{w}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{4\gamma_{w}}{\lambda_{w}}\,r. $$

Moreover $\lambda_{k}(M)\geq\lambda_{w}-r$ , so

$$ \frac{\lambda_{w}}{\lambda_{k}(M)}\leq 1+\frac{2r}{\lambda_{w}},\qquad\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}(M)}\leq\frac{2}{\lambda_{w}} $$

for $r\leq\lambda_{w}/4$ . Combining the numerator perturbation with these denominator bounds yields the local normal-ratio estimate

$$ \rho_{k}^{-}(M;sw)\leq\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w)+\mathfrak{L}_{w}r+\frac{2\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\lambda_{w}}(1-s)\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

The constants in $\mathfrak{L}_{w}$ are intentionally relaxed; the important point is that they are endpoint quantities.

By Assumption 3, the two extra terms in (58) are at most $\mu_{w}/2$ whenever $r\leq r_{w}^{\rm stab}$ . Hence, throughout this endpoint neighborhood,

$$ (1-\delta)-\rho_{k}^{-}(M;sw)\geq\frac{\mu_{w}}{2}, $$

and Proposition 1 again gives (56).

On any interval where (56) holds, differentiating (55) gives

$$ \Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})[\dot{M}_{s}]=\Proj_{T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w), $$

and RIP gives

$$ \left\lVert\Proj_{T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w)\right\rVert_{F}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

Therefore

$$ \left\lVert\dot{M}_{s}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\mu_{w}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

Integrating backward from $s=1$ gives, on any interval where the branch exists inside the endpoint neighborhood,

$$ \left\lVert M_{s}-M_{w}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\mu_{w}}(1-s)\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}r_{w}^{\rm stab}. $$

To formalize the continuation, let $I\subset[0,1]$ be the maximal interval containing $1$ on which the implicit-function branch exists and remains in $\{M:\left\lVert M-M_{w}\right\rVert_{F}<r_{w}^{\rm stab}\}$ . The local implicit-function theorem makes $I$ open relative to $[0,1]$ . The preceding estimate shows that any point of $I$ actually satisfies the stricter bound $\left\lVert M_{s}-M_{w}\right\rVert_{F}\leq r_{w}^{\rm stab}/2$ ; hence limits of branch points remain inside the same neighborhood, the Hessian stays invertible by (56), and the implicit-function theorem extends the branch past the limit. Thus $I$ is also closed, so $I=[0,1]$ . Finally, (57) follows from $r_{w}^{\rm stab}\leq\lambda_{w}/4$ . ∎

#### Theorem 3 (Pointwise rank-stable perturbation bound).

Suppose Assumptions 1–3 hold, and let $M_{0}$ be the paired clean endpoint from Lemma 2. Then

$$ \left\lVert M_{w}-M_{0}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{1+\delta}}{(1-\delta)-\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w)}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

The associated rank- $k$ spectral projector $P_{s}=P_{k}(M_{s})$ , with $P_{w}=P_{1}$ , rotates slowly:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert P_{s}-P_{w}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{8\sqrt{1+\delta}\,(1-s)\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{w})\bigl[(1-\delta)-\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w)\bigr]}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 3.

The rank- $k$ manifold is equipped with the embedded Frobenius metric. By (55), the Riemannian criticality equation is

$$ \grad_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})=0. $$

Differentiate this identity with respect to $s$ . At a critical point, the covariant derivative of the Riemannian gradient in the motion direction $\dot{M}_{s}$ is the Riemannian Hessian, while the explicit derivative of the matrix gradient $G_{s}(M)=H(M-M_{\star})-sN_{w}$ with respect to $s$ is $-N_{w}=-\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{D}{ds}\grad_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s}) \displaystyle=\Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})[\dot{M}_{s}]-\Proj_{T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w). $$

and therefore

$$ \Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})[\dot{M}_{s}]=\Proj_{T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w). $$

This is the intrinsic version of differentiating the pullback criticality equation in local coordinates (Boumal 2023, Proposition 5.45); (Absil et al. 2008, Proposition 5.5.6).

The right-hand side is controlled by RIP. Since every tangent matrix in $T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}$ has rank at most $2k$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\Proj_{T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w)\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\eta\in T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}\\
\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{F}=1\end{subarray}}\left\langle w,\mathcal{A}(\eta)\right\rangle \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

By the Hessian stability condition (56), $\Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{s}(M_{s})$ is self-adjoint and positive definite on $T_{M_{s}}\mathcal{M}_{k}$ , with inverse norm at most $2/\mu_{w}$ . Therefore

$$ \left\lVert\dot{M}_{s}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\mu_{w}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2},\qquad\mu_{w}=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w). $$

Integrating from $s=0$ to $s=1$ proves (60).

For the projector statement, the spectral gap between the $k$ -th and $(k+1)$ -st eigenvalues of $M_{s}$ is $\lambda_{k}(M_{s})$ , because $\rank(M_{s})=k$ . The differential form of the Davis–Kahan/Kato spectral projector bound gives the relaxed estimate (Davis and Kahan 1970; Bhatia 1997)

$$ \left\lVert\dot{P}_{s}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{2\left\lVert\dot{M}_{s}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{s})}\leq\frac{8\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\lambda_{w}\mu_{w}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, $$

where the last step uses (57). Integrating from $s$ to $1$ gives (61). ∎

#### Supporting Chart Diagnostics

Theorem 3 is intrinsic: it controls perturbations in the Frobenius geometry of $\mathcal{M}_{k}$ without choosing local coordinates. We now express the same argument in local coordinates centered at $M_{w}$ . The lemma below shows that its conditioning is governed by the extreme active eigenvalues of $M_{w}$ and deteriorates as $\lambda_{k}(M_{w})$ approaches zero.

#### Lemma 3 (Raw endpoint chart conditioning).

Let

$$ \displaystyle M_{w} \displaystyle=U_{w}\Lambda_{w}U_{w}^{\top}, \displaystyle\Lambda_{w} \displaystyle=\diag(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{k}), \displaystyle\lambda_{1} \displaystyle\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{k}>0. $$

and complete $U_{w}$ to an orthogonal basis $[U_{w}\ U_{w,\perp}]$ . A raw graph chart centered at $M_{w}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(B,Z) \displaystyle=Q(Z)BQ(Z)^{\top}, \displaystyle Q(Z) \displaystyle=(U_{w}+U_{w,\perp}Z)(I+Z^{\top}Z)^{-1/2}. $$

Here $B\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{k}$ , $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$ , $\dot{B}\in\mathbb{S}^{k}$ , and $\dot{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times k}$ . At the base point $(B,Z)=(\Lambda_{w},0)$ , the differential is

$$ \displaystyle D\Phi(\Lambda_{w},0)[\dot{B},\dot{Z}] \displaystyle=U_{w}\dot{B}U_{w}^{\top} \displaystyle+U_{w,\perp}\dot{Z}\Lambda_{w}U_{w}^{\top} \displaystyle+U_{w}\Lambda_{w}\dot{Z}^{\top}U_{w,\perp}^{\top}. $$

With the raw coordinate norm

$$ \left\lVert(\dot{B},\dot{Z})\right\rVert_{\rm raw}^{2}=\left\lVert\dot{B}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\left\lVert\dot{Z}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, $$

the singular values of $D\Phi(\Lambda_{w},0)$ , viewed as a map into Frobenius tangent matrices, lie between

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{-} \displaystyle=\min\{1,\sqrt{2}\,\lambda_{k}(M_{w})\}, \displaystyle\sigma_{+} \displaystyle=\max\{1,\sqrt{2}\,\lambda_{1}(M_{w})\}. $$

Thus the raw chart condition number is

$$ \kappa_{\rm raw}(M_{w})=\frac{\sigma_{+}}{\sigma_{-}}=\frac{\max\{1,\sqrt{2}\,\lambda_{1}(M_{w})\}}{\min\{1,\sqrt{2}\,\lambda_{k}(M_{w})\}}. $$

In raw coordinates, the same argument as Theorem 3 gives

$$ \left\lVert\dot{M}_{s}\right\rVert_{F}\leq 2\kappa_{\rm raw}(M_{w})^{2}\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\mu_{w}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2} $$

at the base point. In tangent-scaled coordinates $K=Z\Lambda_{w}$ , this base-point distortion disappears.

#### Proof of Lemma 3.

Let

$$ W(Z)=U_{w}+U_{w,\perp}Z,\qquad R(Z)=I+Z^{\top}Z, $$

so $Q(Z)=W(Z)R(Z)^{-1/2}$ . For a perturbation $\dot{Z}$ ,

$$ DR(Z)[\dot{Z}]=\dot{Z}^{\top}Z+Z^{\top}\dot{Z}. $$

At $Z=0$ , $DR(0)[\dot{Z}]=0$ , and hence the derivative of the normalization factor $R(Z)^{-1/2}$ vanishes. Therefore

$$ DQ(0)[\dot{Z}]=U_{w,\perp}\dot{Z}. $$

Differentiating $\Phi(B,Z)=Q(Z)BQ(Z)^{\top}$ gives

$$ D\Phi(B,Z)[\dot{B},\dot{Z}]=Q\dot{B}Q^{\top}+\dot{Q}BQ^{\top}+QB\dot{Q}^{\top}. $$

Substituting $Q(0)=U_{w}$ , $B=\Lambda_{w}$ , and $\dot{Q}=U_{w,\perp}\dot{Z}$ proves (62). The three blocks in (62) are Frobenius-orthogonal, so

$$ \left\lVert D\Phi(\Lambda_{w},0)[\dot{B},\dot{Z}]\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\left\lVert\dot{B}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+2\left\lVert\dot{Z}\Lambda_{w}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

Since

$$ \lambda_{k}(M_{w})\left\lVert\dot{Z}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\left\lVert\dot{Z}\Lambda_{w}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\lambda_{1}(M_{w})\left\lVert\dot{Z}\right\rVert_{F}, $$

the singular-value bounds (63) follow. The displayed coordinate velocity bound follows from the coordinate version of the proof: the pulled-back noise gradient is bounded by $\sqrt{1+\delta}\sigma_{+}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}$ , the pulled-back Hessian is lower bounded by $(\mu_{w}/2)\sigma_{-}^{2}$ , and matrix velocity conversion costs another $\sigma_{+}$ . ∎

### B.3 Missing Details of Section 5

#### Proposition 2 (Unused columns force PSD matrix gradient).

Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ be a second-order point of $f_{w}$ . If $\rank(X)<k$ , then

$$ G_{w}(XX^{\top})\succeq 0. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 2.

Choose a unit $v\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ with $Xv=0$ . For any $u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , set $D=uv^{\top}$ . Then $XD^{\top}+DX^{\top}=0$ and $DD^{\top}=uu^{\top}$ . The second-order condition and Lemma 1 give

$$ 0\leq\nabla^{2}f_{w}(X)[D,D]=2u^{\top}G_{w}(XX^{\top})u. $$

Since $u$ is arbitrary, $G_{w}(XX^{\top})\succeq 0$ . ∎

#### Theorem 4 (Rank-deficient points are globally optimal in matrix space).

Let $M=XX^{\top}$ with $\rank(X)<k$ , and suppose $X$ is a second-order point of $f_{w}$ . Then $M$ is a global minimizer of the convex PSD problem

$$ \min_{Z\succeq 0}F_{w}(Z). $$

Consequently:

- 1. If $w=0$ , then $M=M_{\star}$ .

- 2. For general $w$ , if $\rank(M)\leq k$ , then

$$ \left\lVert M-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}}{\sqrt{1-\delta}}. $$

(67)

#### Proof of Theorem 4.

By first-order criticality, $G_{w}(M)X=0$ , hence $G_{w}(M)M=0$ and $\left\langle G_{w}(M),M\right\rangle=0$ . Proposition 2 gives $G_{w}(M)\succeq 0$ . Therefore, for every $Z\succeq 0$ ,

$$ \left\langle G_{w}(M),Z-M\right\rangle=\left\langle G_{w}(M),Z\right\rangle\geq 0. $$

This is the first-order optimality condition for the convex problem (66), so $M$ is a global PSD minimizer.

If $w=0$ , $M_{\star}$ is feasible and has objective value zero. Hence $\mathcal{A}(M-M_{\star})=0$ . Assumption 1 implies $M=M_{\star}$ , since $\rank(M-M_{\star})\leq k+r_{\star}\leq 2k$ .

For general $w$ , use the convex first-order inequality with $Z=M_{\star}$ . Writing $\Delta=M-M_{\star}$ ,

$$ 0\leq\left\langle G_{w}(M),M_{\star}-M\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathcal{A}\Delta-w,-\mathcal{A}\Delta\right\rangle. $$

Thus $\left\lVert\mathcal{A}\Delta\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\langle w,\mathcal{A}\Delta\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\mathcal{A}\Delta\right\rVert_{2}$ , so $\left\lVert\mathcal{A}\Delta\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}$ . Since $\rank(\Delta)\leq k+r_{\star}\leq 2k$ , RIP gives $\sqrt{1-\delta}\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{F}\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{A}\Delta\right\rVert_{2}$ . ∎

#### Remark 3 (Relation to Boumal–Voroninski–Bandeira).

This result is the PSD matrix-sensing specialization of the standard rank-deficiency certificate for Burer–Monteiro factorizations (Burer and Monteiro 2003; Boumal et al. 2016; Boumal et al. 2020); the RIP structure further yields exact recovery in the noiseless case and a noise-linear recovery bound in the noisy case.

### B.4 Full-Rank Points and the Spectral Tail

We now fully discuss the last part of our main theorem. The exact rank-deficiency certificate is no longer available at a full-rank point, but the negative spectral part of the normal block can remain small when the weakest slack direction is small relative to the active spectral floor. Let

$$ M=XX^{\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top},\qquad\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{k}>0, $$

and choose an effective active rank $q\leq k$ with $P_{q}=\sum_{i=1}^{q}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}$ . A negative normal direction can be paired with the weakest active direction. The second-order condition and the unified $2k$ -RIP then limit its negative spectral part by

$$ \left\lVert[P_{q}^{\perp}G_{w}(M)P_{q}^{\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq(1+\delta)\lambda_{k}(M). $$

After normalization by the selected active spectral floor, this becomes

$$ \rho_{q}^{-}(M;w)\leq(1+\delta)\frac{\lambda_{k}(M)}{\lambda_{q}(M)}. $$

#### Proposition 3 (Negative normal curvature is limited by the thinnest slack direction).

Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ be a full-rank second-order point of $f_{w}$ , let

$$ M=XX^{\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top},\qquad\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{k}>0, $$

and choose an effective active rank $q\leq k$ with $P_{q}=\sum_{i=1}^{q}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}$ . Under Assumption 1,

$$ \left\lVert[P_{q}^{\perp}G_{w}(M)P_{q}^{\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq(1+\delta)\lambda_{k}(M). $$

Consequently,

$$ \rho_{q}^{-}(M;w)\leq(1+\delta)\frac{\lambda_{k}(M)}{\lambda_{q}(M)}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 3.

The first-order condition $G_{w}(M)X=0$ implies that $G_{w}(M)$ vanishes on $\operatorname{range}(M)$ . Hence a negative eigenvector of $P_{q}^{\perp}G_{w}(M)P_{q}^{\perp}$ lies in the orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{range}(M)$ . Let $u$ be such a unit vector and let $u_{k}$ be an eigenvector of $M$ associated with $\lambda_{k}(M)$ . Choose factor coordinates so that $Xe_{k}=\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}\,u_{k}$ , and set

$$ D=\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}\,ue_{k}^{\top}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle XD^{\top}+DX^{\top} \displaystyle=\lambda_{k}(u_{k}u^{\top}+uu_{k}^{\top}), \displaystyle\left\lVert XD^{\top}+DX^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=2\lambda_{k}^{2}, \displaystyle DD^{\top} \displaystyle=\lambda_{k}uu^{\top}. $$

If

$$ u^{\top}G_{w}(M)u=-\gamma<0, $$

the second-order condition and Lemma 1 give

$$ 0\leq\nabla^{2}f_{w}(X)[D,D]=\left\lVert\mathcal{A}(XD^{\top}+DX^{\top})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\gamma\lambda_{k}. $$

The matrix $XD^{\top}+DX^{\top}$ has rank at most two, so RIP gives

$$ \left\lVert\mathcal{A}(XD^{\top}+DX^{\top})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta)2\lambda_{k}^{2}. $$

Thus $\gamma\leq(1+\delta)\lambda_{k}$ , proving (70). Dividing by $\lambda_{q}(M)$ gives (71). ∎

For $q<k$ , the spectral ratio $\lambda_{k}(M)/\lambda_{q}(M)$ is therefore an effective-rank diagnostic for normalized negative normal curvature. It controls the weakest slack direction, but not the total discarded tail energy.

#### Corollary 1 (Effective-rank normal-curvature surrogate).

If $M_{w}$ is produced by a full-column-rank second-order point of width $k$ , then for any effective active rank $q<k$ ,

$$ \rho_{q}^{-}(M_{w};w)\leq(1+\delta)\frac{\lambda_{k}(M_{w})}{\lambda_{q}(M_{w})}. $$

This is not the main strict rank-stable theorem, which uses $q=k$ and the directly computed $\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w)$ . It is an effective-rank diagnostic: when the spectral tail ratio $\lambda_{k}(M_{w})/\lambda_{q}(M_{w})$ is small, the normal curvature seen by the active rank- $q$ block is small, but the discarded tail must still be accounted for separately if one truncates to rank $q$ . In particular, $\lambda_{k}/\lambda_{q}$ is the thinnest-tail ratio; it does not by itself control the whole tail energy.

#### Lemma 4 (Deterministic spectral-tail bounds).

Let $M\succeq 0$ have rank at most $k$ , eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{k}\geq 0$ , and fix

$$ 1\leq q<k,\qquad\lambda_{q}(M)>0. $$

Let

$$ M_{q}=\sum_{i=1}^{q}\lambda_{i}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top} $$

be its best rank- $q$ approximation. Then

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert M-M_{q}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle=\lambda_{q+1}(M), \displaystyle\left\lVert M-M_{q}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{i>q}\lambda_{i}(M)^{2}. $$

If $d=k-q$ , then

$$ \frac{\left\lVert M-M_{q}\right\rVert_{F}}{\lambda_{q}(M)}\leq\sqrt{d}\,\frac{\lambda_{q+1}(M)}{\lambda_{q}(M)}. $$

Also,

$$ \frac{\lambda_{k}(M)}{\lambda_{q}(M)}\leq\frac{\left\lVert M-M_{q}\right\rVert_{F}}{\sqrt{d}\,\lambda_{q}(M)}. $$

If, in addition, $\bar{M}\succeq 0$ has rank $q$ and $\left\lVert M-\bar{M}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}<\lambda_{q}(\bar{M})$ , then Weyl’s inequality gives

$$ \frac{\lambda_{k}(M)}{\lambda_{q}(M)}\leq\frac{\left\lVert M-\bar{M}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{q}(\bar{M})-\left\lVert M-\bar{M}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 4.

The identities (73) are the PSD form of the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem (Eckart and Young 1936). Since the $d$ tail eigenvalues $\lambda_{q+1},\ldots,\lambda_{k}$ are all at most $\lambda_{q+1}$ ,

$$ \left\lVert M-M_{q}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i>q}\lambda_{i}^{2}\leq d\,\lambda_{q+1}^{2}, $$

which proves (75). Since the same tail eigenvalues are all at least $\lambda_{k}$ ,

$$ d\,\lambda_{k}^{2}\leq\sum_{i>q}\lambda_{i}^{2}=\left\lVert M-M_{q}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, $$

which proves (76). If $M=\bar{M}+E$ and $\rank(\bar{M})=q$ , Weyl’s inequality yields

$$ \lambda_{q}(M)\geq\lambda_{q}(\bar{M})-\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\qquad\lambda_{k}(M)\leq\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}, $$

because $\lambda_{k}(\bar{M})=0$ for $k>q$ . This proves (77).

∎

For direct recovery relative to the rank- $r_{\star}$ target $M_{\star}$ , the relevant quantity is the numerator of $\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w)$ , rather than its normalization by the active spectral floor. At a full-rank first-order critical point, $G_{w}(M_{w})X_{w}=0$ implies

$$ G_{w}(M_{w})=P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}. $$

We therefore define the absolute negative normal leakage by

$$ b_{w}^{-}:=\left\lVert[P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\lambda_{k}(M_{w})\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w). $$

#### Lemma 5 (Absolute normal leakage).

Let $X_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ be full column rank and first-order critical for $f_{w}$ , let $M_{w}=X_{w}X_{w}^{\top}$ , and let $P_{w}=P_{k}(M_{w})$ . Then

$$ G_{w}(M_{w})=P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}. $$

Define the negative normal leakage amplitude

$$ b_{w}^{-}=\left\lVert[P_{w}^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}^{\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

Equivalently,

$$ b_{w}^{-}=\lambda_{k}(M_{w})\rho_{k}^{-}(M_{w};w). $$

#### Proof of Lemma 5.

First-order criticality gives $G_{w}(M_{w})X_{w}=0$ . Since $X_{w}$ spans $\operatorname{range}(M_{w})$ , this is equivalent to $G_{w}(M_{w})P_{w}=0$ . By symmetry also $P_{w}G_{w}(M_{w})=0$ , so $G_{w}(M_{w})$ is supported on the normal block. Equation (80) is the definition of $\rho_{k}^{-}$ in (6) with $q=k$ . ∎

Lemma 5 isolates the adverse part of the normal block at a full-rank critical point: $b_{w}^{-}$ measures its absolute spectral amplitude, while $\rho_{k}^{-}$ is the corresponding normalization by the weakest active eigenvalue. To convert this local quantity into a recovery estimate, we must also control how much of the target matrix lies outside $\operatorname{range}(M_{w})$ .The next lemma bounds this target-subspace leakage directly by the reconstruction error.

#### Lemma 6 (Target subspace leakage).

Let $M_{\star}\succeq 0$ have rank $1\leq r_{\star}\leq k$ , let

$$ \lambda_{\star}=\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})>0, $$

and let $M_{w}\succeq 0$ have range projector $P_{w}$ . Then

$$ \tr(P_{w}^{\perp}M_{\star}P_{w}^{\perp})\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{\star}}\left\lVert M_{w}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 6.

Write

$$ M_{\star}=U_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}U_{\star}^{\top} $$

and set $E=M_{w}-M_{\star}$ . Since $P_{w}^{\perp}M_{w}=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P_{w}^{\perp}U_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}^{1/2} \displaystyle=P_{w}^{\perp}M_{\star}U_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}^{-1/2} \displaystyle=-P_{w}^{\perp}EU_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}^{-1/2}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\tr(P_{w}^{\perp}M_{\star}P_{w}^{\perp}) \displaystyle=\left\lVert P_{w}^{\perp}U_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}^{1/2}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\left\lVert P_{w}^{\perp}EU_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\Lambda_{\star}^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda_{\star}}\left\lVert M_{w}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, $$

which proves (81).

∎

Lemmas 5 and 6 now connect the normal geometry to recovery. Writing $E=M_{w}-M_{\star}$ and $\lambda_{\star}=\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})$ , first-order criticality gives

$$ \left\langle G_{w}(M_{w}),E\right\rangle=-\left\langle G_{w}(M_{w}),M_{\star}\right\rangle\leq\frac{b_{w}^{-}}{\lambda_{\star}}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

Meanwhile, RIP lower-bounds the data-fit contribution by $(1-\delta)\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2}$ , up to the measurement-noise term. Hence the normal leakage can be absorbed whenever $(1-\delta)-b_{w}^{-}/\lambda_{\star}>0$ . The following lemma formalizes the resulting recovery bound.

#### Lemma 7 (Normal leakage recovery bound).

Assume the unified $2k$ -RIP in Assumption 1, and let $M_{\star}\succeq 0$ have rank $1\leq r_{\star}\leq k$ . Let $X_{w}$ be a full-column-rank first-order critical point of $f_{w}$ , and let $M_{w}=X_{w}X_{w}^{\top}$ . Define $b_{w}^{-}$ by (78), set

$$ \mu_{\rm leak}=1-\delta-\frac{b_{w}^{-}}{\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})}, $$

and assume $\mu_{\rm leak}>0$ . Then

$$ \left\lVert M_{w}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\mu_{\rm leak}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 7.

Let $E=M_{w}-M_{\star}$ , $G=G_{w}(M_{w})$ , and $\lambda_{\star}=\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})$ . By first-order criticality, $GX_{w}=0$ , and hence $GM_{w}=0$ . Therefore,

$$ \left\langle G,E\right\rangle=-\left\langle G,M_{\star}\right\rangle. $$

Since $G$ is supported on $P_{w}^{\perp}$ , Lemmas 5 and 6 give

$$ \displaystyle-\left\langle G,M_{\star}\right\rangle \displaystyle\leq b_{w}^{-}\,\tr(P_{w}^{\perp}M_{\star}P_{w}^{\perp}) \displaystyle\leq\frac{b_{w}^{-}}{\lambda_{\star}}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

On the other hand,

$$ \left\langle G,E\right\rangle=\left\lVert\mathcal{A}(E)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\langle w,\mathcal{A}(E)\right\rangle. $$

Since $\rank(E)\leq k+r_{\star}\leq 2k$ , RIP and Cauchy–Schwarz imply

$$ (1-\delta)\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}+\frac{b_{w}^{-}}{\lambda_{\star}}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. $$

Rearranging and using (82) gives

$$ \mu_{\rm leak}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{F}, $$

which proves (83).

∎

Another ingredient controls the portion of the lower-rank target that lies outside $\operatorname{range}(M_{w})$ . This target-subspace leakage is controlled by the current recovery error. Combining that estimate with $b_{w}^{-}$ and the unified $2k$ -RIP gives the direct full-rank recovery certificate below.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.

Part (1) is Theorem 4. Part (2) is Theorem 3, whose strict full-rank case uses active rank $k$ . Part (3) is Lemma 5 followed by Lemma 7.

∎

## Appendix C Trajectory Case Study: Full-Rank Shadowing from Small Initialization

This section studies robustness along the whole GD path rather than at one critical endpoint. Therefore the clean reference is not a single matrix $M_{0}$ . It is the time-indexed noiseless trajectory

$$ M_{t}^{0}=X_{t}^{0}X_{t}^{0\top}, $$

run from the same initialization as the noisy trajectory

$$ M_{t}^{w}=X_{t}^{w}X_{t}^{w\top}. $$

The trajectory robustness question is

$$ \Delta_{t}=\left\lVert M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

Throughout this section we focus on the full-rank-to-full-rank regime with $k\leq n$ : for the time window under discussion, both $X_{t}^{0}$ and $X_{t}^{w}$ remain full column rank, so $M_{t}^{0}$ and $M_{t}^{w}$ lie on the rank- $k$ PSD manifold. The role of the normal-curvature ratio is now dynamic. A small $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ , defined in (85), together with the local Hessian check below, indicates that the rank- $k$ tangent dynamics around $M_{t}^{w}$ are well conditioned, so measurement noise cannot separate the noisy and noiseless trajectories too much during the next steps.

### C.1 Clean and Noisy GD Paths

Let $N_{0}=0$ and $N_{w}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w$ . Starting from the same small random initialization $X_{0}^{0}=X_{0}^{w}=\alpha G$ , define

$$ \displaystyle X_{t+1}^{\zeta} \displaystyle=\left(I+\eta[H(M_{\star}-M_{t}^{\zeta})+N_{\zeta}]\right)X_{t}^{\zeta}, \displaystyle M_{t}^{\zeta} \displaystyle=X_{t}^{\zeta}(X_{t}^{\zeta})^{\top},\qquad\zeta\in\{0,w\}. $$

The clean recursion is the one studied by Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021), up to normalization constants. In their notation the target is $M_{\star}=X_{\star}X_{\star}^{\top}$ , the factor condition number is

$$ \kappa_{X}=\frac{\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sigma_{\min}(X_{\star})}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})}{\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})}}, $$

the search width is $k>r_{\star}$ , $X_{0}=\alpha G$ with entries of $G$ distributed as $N(0,1/\sqrt{k})$ , and the step size satisfies $\eta\lesssim\kappa_{X}^{-4}\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{-2}$ . Equivalently, if $\kappa_{M}=\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})/\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star})$ , then the step size is of order $\kappa_{M}^{-2}\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})^{-1}$ . Their Theorem 3.3 assumes $k>r_{\star}$ , splits into the regimes $k\geq 2r_{\star}$ and $r_{\star}<k<2r_{\star}$ , and requires rank- $(2r_{\star}+1)$ RIP with constant of order at most $1/(\kappa_{X}^{4}\sqrt{r_{\star}})$ , together with explicit small upper bounds on $\alpha$ . It proves a finite-time early-stopped proximity bound for the clean iterates. In the $k\geq 2r_{\star}$ case, the normalized error after the prescribed number of iterations is bounded by a polynomial factor times $(\alpha/\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}})^{21/16}$ . The exactly parameterized case $k=r_{\star}$ is treated separately in their Theorem 3.4.

The clean result is used here as a reference path. The new object is the shadowing error $\Delta_{t}$ between (84) with and without $w$ . No critical-point comparison is needed.

### C.2 Rank- $k$ Rho and a Shadowing Bound

For a full-rank noisy iterate $M_{t}^{w}$ , let $P_{t}^{w}=P_{k}(M_{t}^{w})$ . In this section

$$ G_{w}(M)=H(M-M_{\star})-N_{w} $$

is the noisy matrix gradient. Define

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{k,t}^{-} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert\bigl[P_{t}^{w,\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P_{t}^{w,\perp}\bigr]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})}, \displaystyle\mu_{t}^{\rho} \displaystyle=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k,t}^{-}. $$

This is the same full-rank denominator as in the endpoint perturbation theorem, but now it is evaluated along the noisy trajectory. The following deterministic shadowing lemma is the trajectory analogue of the endpoint bound. Because trajectory points are not critical points, $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ should be read as a pointwise lower-margin estimate for the local linearized rank- $k$ map, not as an automatic theorem about every GD step.

To make the bridge explicit, let

$$ \Psi_{t}^{0}(M)=\mathcal{R}_{M}\!\left(-\eta\,\grad_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{0}(M)\right) $$

be the noiseless rank- $k$ manifold step in a local chart, with any smooth first-order retraction $\mathcal{R}$ . A sufficient check for the contraction used below is for every $\eta_{M}\in T_{M_{t}^{w}}\mathcal{M}_{k}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\eta_{M},\Hess_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}F_{0}(M_{t}^{w})[\eta_{M}]\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq\mu_{t}^{\rho}\left\lVert\eta_{M}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, \displaystyle\eta L_{t} \displaystyle\leq 1. $$

where $L_{t}$ is a local smoothness bound for the charted gradient map. For the local quadratic model, and for the charted map after absorbing higher-order retraction terms into the local check, this gives $\left\lVert D\Psi_{t}^{0}\right\rVert\leq 1-\eta\mu_{t}^{\rho}$ . Thus the Hessian Rayleigh quotient is the actual trajectory certificate. The ratio (85) is the rank- $k$ normal-block diagnostic that explains when the check should become favorable; at endpoint-critical or tangent-critical points it reduces to the same normal-curvature margin used in Proposition 1.

#### Lemma 8 (Full-rank trajectory shadowing controlled by $\rho$ ).

Fix a time horizon $T$ . Suppose that the paired clean and noisy trajectories remain in a common full-rank $k$ -dimensional chart for $0\leq t\leq T$ . Assume that the local Hessian/smoothness check (86) holds, so the noiseless chart map satisfies

$$ \left\lVert D\Psi_{t}^{0}\right\rVert\leq 1-\eta\mu_{t}^{\rho}. $$

Then the noisy and noiseless matrix iterates obey

$$ \Delta_{t+1}\leq(1-\eta\mu_{t}^{\rho})\Delta_{t}+\eta\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, $$

and therefore

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\eta\prod_{\ell=j+1}^{t-1}(1-\eta\mu_{\ell}^{\rho}). $$

If $\mu_{t}^{\rho}\geq\underline{\mu}>0$ on the whole window and $\eta\underline{\mu}\leq 1$ , then

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}\left(1-(1-\eta\underline{\mu})^{t}\right)\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

#### Proof.

The only first-order difference between the two local rank- $k$ maps at the same matrix is the tangent projection of $N_{w}=\mathcal{A}^{\ast}w$ . RIP gives

$$ \left\lVert\Proj_{T_{M_{t}^{w}}\mathcal{M}_{k}}N_{w}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, $$

because tangent matrices have rank at most $2k$ . By assumption, the computed rank- $k$ margin $\mu_{t}^{\rho}=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ certifies the one-step tangent contraction. Combining this contraction of the clean map with the additive noise perturbation gives (87). Iterating the scalar recursion gives (88), and the geometric sum gives (89). ∎

Lemma 8 is the clean trajectory philosophy. The object $M_{t}^{0}$ is the clean iterate at the same time $t$ , not the clean critical endpoint used earlier. The time-varying stability margin is $\mu_{t}^{\rho}=(1-\delta)-\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ , where the ratio $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ contains the active floor $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})$ in its denominator. Early times with a poor rank- $k$ margin contribute large terms to the sum in (88); times with a strong margin damp all previous noise.

### C.3 Stöger–Soltanolkotabi Variables and a $\rho$ -Proxy

The remaining question is how the dynamics make the $\rho$ -margin better or worse. The clean analysis of Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021) introduces a signal/slack split that is useful for interpreting this. Their “noise” term is an internal over-parameterized slack factor, not observation noise $w$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle M_{\star} \displaystyle=V_{\star}\Lambda_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}, \displaystyle\qquad P_{\star} \displaystyle=V_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}, \displaystyle\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle=\lambda_{r_{\star}}(M_{\star}), \displaystyle\qquad\kappa_{X} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sigma_{\min}(X_{\star})}. $$

For a clean iterate $X_{t}^{0}$ , take the compact SVD

$$ V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}=\widetilde{V}_{t}\Sigma_{t}W_{t}^{\top},\qquad W_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times r_{\star}},\qquad W_{t}^{\top}W_{t}=I, $$

and complete $W_{t}$ to $[W_{t}\ W_{t,\perp}]$ . Following their Section 5.1, write

$$ \displaystyle S_{t} \displaystyle=X_{t}^{0}W_{t},\qquad N_{t}=X_{t}^{0}W_{t,\perp}, \displaystyle X_{t}^{0} \displaystyle=S_{t}W_{t}^{\top}+N_{t}W_{t,\perp}^{\top}. $$

By Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021, Lemma 5.1), the slack factor has column span orthogonal to $V_{\star}$ , and, whenever $V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}$ has full row rank, $S_{t}$ has rank $r_{\star}$ while $N_{t}$ has rank at most $k-r_{\star}$ . Let $V_{S_{t}}$ denote an orthonormal basis for $\operatorname{col}(S_{t})$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle s_{t} \displaystyle=\sigma_{\min}(S_{t}),\quad\nu_{t}=\left\lVert N_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\quad\phi_{t}=\frac{s_{t}^{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}, \displaystyle\xi_{t} \displaystyle=\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\quad\chi_{t}=\frac{\nu_{t}^{2}}{s_{t}^{2}}, \displaystyle\varepsilon_{t} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\top}(M_{t}^{0}-M_{\star})\right\rVert_{F}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

The angle $\xi_{t}$ is the clean signal-factor angle; in Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021), Lemma 9.1 grows the projected signal singular value, Lemma 9.2 controls the internal slack factor, and Lemma 9.3 gives the direct angle recurrence. The auxiliary $\varepsilon_{t}$ is used below only to quote their Phase III refinement; it is not a separate term in the four-metric dashboard. With sensing distortion one also uses the top $r_{\star}$ -dimensional spectral space $P_{H}$ of $H(M_{\star})$ and the upper proxy

$$ \theta_{t}=\left\lVert V_{S_{t}}^{\perp}P_{H}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\left\lVert P_{H}^{\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\qquad\xi_{t}\leq\theta_{t}, $$

where the second term is controlled by Davis–Kahan when $\left\lVert H(M_{\star})-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\ll\lambda_{\star}$ .

The strict full-rank robustness ratio uses the smallest rank- $k$ eigenvalue of the noisy iterate. Normalize this floor by the signal scale:

$$ \psi_{t}^{w}=\frac{\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

The normal block is easiest to read through one subspace metric. For the mathematical bound we use the target alignment

$$ m_{t}^{w}=\left\lVert P_{t}^{w,\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}. $$

This measures how much of the true signal space is still visible from the noisy normal space. It is small when the noisy rank- $k$ range contains the target signal space. If $P_{\star}$ is unavailable and the spectral surrogate $P_{H}$ is used instead, then

$$ m_{t}^{w}\leq\left\lVert P_{t}^{w,\perp}P_{H}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\left\lVert P_{H}^{\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}, $$

and the second term is controlled by Davis–Kahan under the spectral closeness condition stated above. The normalized external noise level is

$$ \eta_{w}=\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

On a bootstrap window where Lemma 8 keeps $\Delta_{t}=O(\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2})$ , the clean/noisy path discrepancy is folded into the same relaxed noise scale. The signal-floor/slack part is represented by the measured floor $\psi_{t}^{w}$ and the slack tail

$$ \tau_{t}=\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\,\chi_{t}\phi_{t}=\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\,\frac{\nu_{t}^{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

Thus $\tau_{t}$ is not another signal-growth variable; it is the Frobenius-sized energy of the $k-r_{\star}$ internal slack directions, normalized by the target spectral floor.

The following lemma is the promised mathematical bound. It has two fixed constants, not two new trajectory metrics. The constant $c_{\rm sh}$ says that the noisy and clean paths are already in the small-noise shadowing window, and $c_{\rm sig}$ is the clean signal-block radius. For example, $c_{\rm sig}=5\sqrt{r_{\star}}\kappa_{X}^{2}$ is valid whenever $\left\lVert S_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ , because then

$$ \left\lVert S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}\leq 5\sqrt{r_{\star}}\,\kappa_{X}^{2}\lambda_{\star}. $$

#### Lemma 9 (Four-metric upper bound for the trajectory $\rho$ ).

Assume $k>r_{\star}$ . Fix a full-rank time $t$ in the trajectory window. Suppose

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{t} \displaystyle=\left\lVert M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0}\right\rVert_{F}\leq c_{\rm sh}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}, \displaystyle\left\lVert S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle\leq c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{k,t}^{-} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+(1+\delta)\tau_{t}+\delta c_{\rm sig}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left(1+c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\right)\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}}. $$

Equivalently, the margin in Lemma 8 is positive whenever the numerator in (96) is smaller than $(1-\delta)\psi_{t}^{w}$ . If the surrogate $P_{H}$ is used, replace $(m_{t}^{w})^{2}$ by

$$ \left(\left\lVert P_{t}^{w,\perp}P_{H}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\left\lVert P_{H}^{\perp}P_{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\right)^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $P=P_{t}^{w}$ and

$$ B=P^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P^{\perp}. $$

Since $\left\lVert[B]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\left\lVert v\right\rVert=1,\ v\in\operatorname{range}(P^{\perp})}[-v^{\top}Bv]_{+}$ , it is enough to bound the negative Rayleigh quotient on a unit normal vector $v$ . Using $M_{t}^{0}=S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}+N_{t}N_{t}^{\top}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-v^{\top}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})v \displaystyle=-v^{\top}H(M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0})v \displaystyle-v^{\top}H(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v \displaystyle-v^{\top}H(N_{t}N_{t}^{\top})v \displaystyle+v^{\top}N_{w}v. $$

The shadowing and observation-noise terms satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}H(M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0})v\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\Delta_{t} \displaystyle\leq c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\,\lambda_{\star}\eta_{w}, \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}N_{w}v\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\star}\eta_{w}. $$

For the active signal block, restricted polarization gives

$$ \displaystyle v^{\top}H(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v \displaystyle\geq v^{\top}(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v \displaystyle-\delta\left\lVert S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

This polarization step uses only the unified $2k$ -RIP, because $\rank(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})\leq 2r_{\star}$ and the trajectory case has $k>r_{\star}$ , so $2r_{\star}+1\leq 2k$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\left[-v^{\top}H(S_{t}S_{t}^{\top}-M_{\star})v\right]_{+} \displaystyle\leq\left[v^{\top}(M_{\star}-S_{t}S_{t}^{\top})v\right]_{+} \displaystyle+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle\leq v^{\top}M_{\star}v+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{1}(M_{\star})\left\lVert P_{\star}v\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star} \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\star}\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2} \displaystyle+\delta c_{\rm sig}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Finally,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert v^{\top}H(N_{t}N_{t}^{\top})v\right\rvert \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert N_{t}N_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle\leq(1+\delta)\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\nu_{t}^{2} \displaystyle=(1+\delta)\tau_{t}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Combining these four estimates and dividing by $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})=\psi_{t}^{w}\lambda_{\star}$ gives (96). ∎

Combining Lemmas 8 and 9 gives the explicit trajectory perturbation bound. Define the four-metric upper envelope

$$ \displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{k,t} \displaystyle=\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+(1+\delta)\tau_{t}+\delta c_{\rm sig}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left(1+c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\right)\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}}, \displaystyle\bar{\mu}_{t} \displaystyle=(1-\delta)-\bar{\rho}_{k,t}. $$

On any time window where the hypotheses of Lemma 9 hold at each time and the local Hessian check in (86) holds, if $\bar{\mu}_{t}>0$ , then $\mu_{t}^{\rho}\geq\bar{\mu}_{t}$ and

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\eta\prod_{\ell=j+1}^{t-1}(1-\eta\bar{\mu}_{\ell}). $$

In particular, if $\bar{\mu}_{t}\geq\underline{\mu}>0$ on the window, then

$$ \left\lVert M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}. $$

This is the actual robustness statement in the trajectory section: alignment, slack, noise, and the active floor determine $\bar{\rho}_{k,t}$ , and the gap $\bar{\mu}_{t}=(1-\delta)-\bar{\rho}_{k,t}$ determines the perturbation size. The bootstrap form is non-circular. Fix a desired uniform margin $\underline{\mu}>0$ and set

$$ c_{\rm sh}=\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta}}{\underline{\mu}}. $$

If, with this predetermined value of $c_{\rm sh}$ , the envelope (97) satisfies

$$ \bar{\rho}_{k,t}\leq 1-\delta-\underline{\mu}\qquad\text{for every }0\leq t\leq T, $$

then (99) gives

$$ \Delta_{t}\leq c_{\rm sh}\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{2}\qquad\text{for every }0\leq t\leq T. $$

Thus the shadowing condition used inside Lemma 9 is proved by induction on the same window, rather than assumed after the fact.

The exact ratio $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ remains directly computable from (85). Lemma 9 gives the relaxed four-metric upper bound

$$ \widehat{\rho}_{k,t}^{\rm traj}:=\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+\tau_{t}+\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}}. $$

This is the readable version of (96) after folding the fixed RIP-bias term $\delta c_{\rm sig}$ and the fixed shadowing constant $c_{\rm sh}$ into constants. The measured certificate remains $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ , but now the section has an explicit upper bound:

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{k,t}^{-} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa_{X}^{2}(m_{t}^{w})^{2}+(1+\delta)\tau_{t}+\delta c_{\rm sig}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left(1+c_{\rm sh}\sqrt{1+\delta}\right)\eta_{w}}{\psi_{t}^{w}} \displaystyle\approx\widehat{\rho}_{k,t}^{\rm traj}. $$

The denominator $\psi_{t}^{w}$ is the active full-rank floor. The middle term is the slack tail created by the extra $k-r_{\star}$ columns. Here “active” means active in the rank- $k$ chart, not necessarily signal-aligned with $M_{\star}$ ; when $k>r_{\star}$ , the floor may be carried by the thinnest retained slack direction. The remaining noise term $\eta_{w}$ absorbs the small perturbation effects we are deliberately not separating in this relaxed dashboard. Even excellent signal variables do not certify strict full-rank robustness if $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})$ is still microscopic.

To see (100), set $P=P_{t}^{w}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle P^{\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P^{\perp} \displaystyle=P^{\perp}H(M_{t}^{w}-M_{t}^{0})P^{\perp} \displaystyle+P^{\perp}H(M_{t}^{0}-M_{\star})P^{\perp} \displaystyle-P^{\perp}N_{w}P^{\perp}. $$

For a unit vector $v\in\operatorname{range}(P_{t}^{w,\perp})$ , Cauchy–Schwarz and RIP give $\left\lvert v^{\top}N_{w}v\right\rvert\lesssim\lambda_{\star}\eta_{w}$ . The clean residual is controlled by the single misalignment metric $m_{t}^{w}$ : larger $m_{t}^{w}$ means the noisy normal space still sees signal directions and can therefore contain more negative normal curvature. The slack block has Frobenius norm at most

$$ \sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\nu_{t}^{2}=\tau_{t}\lambda_{\star}. $$

Dividing the corresponding rigorous estimate by $\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})=\psi_{t}^{w}\lambda_{\star}$ is precisely Lemma 9. The simplified display (100) only suppresses the fixed constants from (96); the exact robustness certificate is still the measured $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ together with the Hessian check (86).

### C.4 Clean Phase Dynamics and the Evolution of the $\rho$ -Proxy

The robustness quantity in this section is always the strict full-rank margin $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ from (85). The proxy (100) only explains its moving parts. Once the measured ratio gives a positive margin and the local Hessian check passes, Lemma 8 converts that margin into the shadowing bound (88). The phase story below is therefore a story about the dashboard in (100): how the single misalignment metric $m_{t}^{w}$ , the slack tail $\tau_{t}$ , the noise level $\eta_{w}$ , and the measured rank- $k$ floor $\psi_{t}^{w}$ evolve.

#### Phase I: spectral alignment.

The first phase is controlled by the power-method comparison in Stöger and Soltanolkotabi (2021, Lemmas 8.1–8.2). They compare GD to the linearized iterate

$$ \widetilde{X}_{t}=(I+\eta H(M_{\star}))^{t}X_{0} $$

and show that $X_{t}^{0}$ remains close to $\widetilde{X}_{t}$ while the iterate is small. Their Lemma 8.3 gives SVD perturbation bounds for the approximate power iterate $Z_{t}X_{0}+E_{t}$ ; Lemma 8.4 translates top-left-singular-space alignment into properties of $X_{t}^{0}W_{t}$ and $X_{t}^{0}W_{t,\perp}$ ; Lemma 8.5 combines these two steps, under spectral closeness $H(M_{\star})=M_{\star}+\widetilde{E}$ , small $\left\lVert\widetilde{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}/\lambda_{\star}$ , and the corresponding small power-method error parameter, into lower bounds on $\sigma_{\min}(X_{t}^{0}W_{t})$ , upper bounds on $\left\lVert X_{t}^{0}W_{t,\perp}\right\rVert$ , and angle bounds for $\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ . Their Theorem 8.8 supplies the Gaussian smallest-singular-value lower bound for an $r_{\star}\times k$ Gaussian matrix with entries normalized by $1/\sqrt{k}$ :

$$ \sigma_{\min}(G)\geq\varepsilon\,\frac{\sqrt{k}-\sqrt{r_{\star}-1}}{\sqrt{k}} $$

with probability at least $1-(C\varepsilon)^{k-r_{\star}+1}-e^{-ck}$ . This is the probabilistic source of improved initial overlap under over-parameterization.

In the dashboard (100), Phase I primarily reduces the clean component of $m_{t}^{w}$ . More precisely, Lemma 8.5 controls the clean subspace angle through $\xi_{t}$ after the approximate power-method phase, while the small-noise/bootstrap condition keeps the noisy component at the $\eta_{w}$ scale. In this relaxed view, Phase I is best viewed as subspace preparation: the trajectory has learned where the signal is, but the full-rank chart may still be fragile.

#### Phase II: saddle avoidance and signal-floor growth.

After alignment, the clean trajectory obeys the signal-floor growth inequality (Stöger and Soltanolkotabi 2021, Lemma 9.1)

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t+1}^{0}) \displaystyle\geq\left(1+\frac{1}{4}\eta\lambda_{\star}\right)\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}) \displaystyle-\eta\,\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0})^{3}. $$

under their step-size, angle, norm, and RIP-error conditions. While this projected signal floor is below signal scale, and while $\xi_{t}=\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ remains small, it is comparable to $\sigma_{\min}(S_{t})$ up to the principal-angle factor $\sqrt{1-\xi_{t}^{2}}$ . Hence a useful reading is

$$ s_{t+1}\gtrsim s_{t}(1+c\eta\lambda_{\star}),\qquad\phi_{t+1}\gtrsim\phi_{t}(1+c\eta\lambda_{\star})^{2}. $$

The same analysis controls the slack factor $\nu_{t}=\left\lVert N_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ and the signal angle (Stöger and Soltanolkotabi 2021, Lemmas 9.2–9.3). In the proof of Theorem 9.6, starting from a post-spectral time $t_{0}$ with initial signal scale $\gamma$ , Phase II is summarized by inductive bounds of the form

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\min}(V_{\star}^{\top}X_{t}^{0}) \displaystyle\gtrsim(1+c\eta\lambda_{\star})^{t-t_{0}}\gamma, \displaystyle\nu_{t} \displaystyle\lesssim(1+c_{\rm slack}\eta\lambda_{\star})^{t-t_{0}}\gamma, \displaystyle\xi_{t} \displaystyle\lesssim\kappa_{X}^{-2}. $$

Therefore the clean signal floor grows while the slack ratio $\chi_{t}=\nu_{t}^{2}/s_{t}^{2}$ and the angle remain controlled. In the dashboard (100), this is the favorable middle regime: $m_{t}^{w}$ is small because the surrogate signal space is aligned, while $\tau_{t}=\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\chi_{t}\phi_{t}$ is harmless only if the product $\chi_{t}\phi_{t}$ remains small relative to $\psi_{t}^{w}$ . The noise level $\eta_{w}$ is the fixed floor. The measured denominator $\psi_{t}^{w}$ can become meaningful if the smallest rank- $k$ direction is no longer microscopic. The caveat is the slack tail

$$ (1+\delta)\tau_{t}=(1+\delta)\sqrt{k-r_{\star}}\,\frac{\nu_{t}^{2}}{\lambda_{\star}}. $$

Lemma 9.2 controls slack relative to the signal factor, but the proxy cares about $\tau_{t}/\psi_{t}^{w}$ . Thus slack stays harmless only when its normalized energy remains small relative to the measured rank- $k$ floor. For strict full-rank robustness, the decisive test is still whether the computed

$$ \rho_{k,t}^{-}=\frac{\left\lVert[P_{t}^{w,\perp}G_{w}(M_{t}^{w})P_{t}^{w,\perp}]_{-}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}(M_{t}^{w})} $$

falls below $1-\delta$ . Phase II is the period in which this can happen: the numerator becomes more signal-aligned, while the denominator becomes acceptable if the smallest retained rank- $k$ direction, possibly a slack direction relative to $M_{\star}$ , has grown enough to make the rank- $k$ chart well conditioned.

#### Phase III: local refinement and slack risk.

Once $s_{t}$ reaches signal scale, the active reconstruction error contracts (Stöger and Soltanolkotabi 2021, Lemma 9.5):

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\top}(M_{\star}-M_{t+1}^{0})\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle\leq(1-c\eta\lambda_{\star})\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\top}(M_{\star}-M_{t}^{0})\right\rVert_{F} \displaystyle+C\eta\lambda_{\star}\left\lVert N_{t}N_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}. $$

Their Theorem 9.6 then combines Phase II and Phase III. Its post-spectral hypotheses include $\min\{k,n\}>r_{\star}$ , bounded iterate norm, small slack, alignment $\left\lVert V_{\star}^{\perp}V_{S_{t_{0}}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lesssim\kappa_{X}^{-2}$ , an initial signal scale

$$ \gamma\leq\frac{c\,\sigma_{\min}(X_{\star})}{\min\{k,n\}\kappa_{X}^{2}}, $$

and a rank- $(2r_{\star}+1)$ RIP constant of order at most $1/(\kappa_{X}^{4}\sqrt{r_{\star}})$ . Under these hypotheses, the additional iteration count is

$$ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\eta\lambda_{\star}}\log\!\left(\max\left\{1,\frac{\kappa_{X}r_{\star}}{\min\{k,n\}-r_{\star}}\right\}\frac{\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert}{\gamma}\right)\right) $$

and the clean error is bounded by a polynomial factor times $(\gamma/\left\lVert X_{\star}\right\rVert)^{21/16}$ . In the dashboard (100), Phase III no longer introduces a separate active-error metric; the four-metric view keeps $\eta_{w}$ as the fixed external noise floor and tracks the remaining risk through $\tau_{t}$ . This is good for clean active reconstruction, but it is not by itself a strict full-rank robustness certificate. The slack tail can still dominate if the extra columns fail to decay relative to $\psi_{t}^{w}$ . Then $\tau_{t}/\psi_{t}^{w}$ can flatten or increase, and the strict full-rank $\rho$ -margin stops improving.

The trajectory-aware stopping rule is therefore simple: continue while the measured $\rho_{k,t}^{-}$ decreases or the shadowing bound (88) tightens; stop, damp, or truncate once the full-rank $\rho$ -margin stops improving.
